rv.q: His account of something that happened to him as a teenager unfurls with the can’t-look-away quality of a slow-motion crash.
Everything’s Fine is emotionally resonant, engagingly performed, immaculately presented and thoughtful entertainment.
Everything’s Fine is a superior entertainment and a satisfying evening in the theater.
It's a master class in good storytelling.
Even if you don’t detect the irony in the title Everything’s Fine, you likely won’t be prepared for the horror show that unfolds in Douglas McGrath’s deceptively folksy, charming one-man play.
The only thing Lithgow left out is that McGrath could have used a net, since he falls off that high wire frequently in this entertaining but ultimately troubling evening.
It's a rambling evening, its incidental pleasures mixed with longueur, falling short of the emotional impact that McGrath seemingly aims for.

The size of the theater and the fact that McGrath often breaks the 'fourth wall,' talking directly to his audience, give this 90-minute, intermissionless work an intimacy and a charm that makes it appear more like a friendly, shared recollection than hard drama.

In Everything’s Fine, McGrath is a fabulously engaging storyteller, but everything wasn’t fine inside me as I left wondering when this internalized trauma will be unpacked and worked through, not simply tossed aside, like an empty blue envelope.
It just doesn’t birth very compelling theater.

cn.t: McGrath's charming storytelling and folksy humor engage audiences, but critics are divided on whether his breezy tone serves or undermines the darker autobiographical material at the show's core.
